newsitem.title: USA: IPO VIEW - Meager returns keep damper on demand.
newsitem.headline: IPO VIEW - Meager returns keep damper on demand.

text.p: Relatively meager returns have kept demand in check for initial public offerings and could translate into lower prices and possible buying opportunities for smaller investors.

For companies that went public in 1996, average gains through last week were 14.5 percent, according to Securities Data Co. That looks paltry compared to gains of 26 percent, 20 percent and 22 percent for the Dow Industrials, the Standard & Poor's 500 Index and the Nasdaq Composite, respectively.

But for companies gone public this year, the average gain is 7.45 percent. That compares more favorably to the major averages in 1997, but many IPO buyers and sellers expect a gain of ten percent as a rule of thumb for a successful IPO.
And those gains come hard-won, on the back of repeated price cuts forced by weak demand.
Of the 114 IPOs priced so far this year, 20 priced above the range and nearly twice that number, 37, priced below expectations with the remainder pricing where expected.
"Usually it's a bell curve, with most deals in the middle and an equal number of deals on either side," said Richard Peterson of Securities Data.

The lower prices means individual investors have a better chance at buying into an initial public offering, but they should keep their pencils sharpened and carefully pour over prospectuses as high-quality companies have been scarce, some analysts say. Securities Data said 29 percent of the companies that went public this year have lost money.
"There's no specific trend right now other than 'Big is in'," said John Fitzgibbon, editor of the IPO Aftermarket.

Spooked by the poor returns and concerns about the broader stock market, large institutional investors have been shying away from small, high-risk deals and choosing large stock offerings that offer the safety of stronger financial histories and better liquidity during a possible downturn.

"(Buyers have) been very discerning. They are looking very closely at transactions and are exercising price discipline," said Brian Hehir, co-head of equity markets at Merrill Lynch & Co. "Backlog is pretty low for middle March though. We should be approaching peak backlog at this point with the end of the quarter coming," he said.
Analysts see no discernible end in sight for the cautious mood, which has meant bargain-basement prices on IPOs, though dollar volume remains strong.

"My sense is what we have is people missing the sizzle. We had some quite large deals done very quietly in the first quarter," said Hehir, noting solid gains for Nationwide Financial's $480 million IPO and Trigon's $200 million market debut.

IPO activity was quiet last week, with nine deals raising $362 million, according to MCM CorporateWatch. After a mostly lackluster week, NeoMagic Corp and Guitar Center Inc both posted sharply higher opening premiums of about 20 percent on Friday.

NeoMagic, which makes multimedia accelerators for personal computer notebooks, had been expected to perform well based on its very low offering price. The deal was initially filed to price at between $7 to $9, but finally sold for $12 a share.

"It did very well, but of course it did at that discount. When was the last time you saw a deal come out of Morgan Stanley at $7?," one underwriter asked. She said that the very low price first set by Morgan Stanley could signal that underwriters have begun to discount IPOs sharply from the very first, which could signal a healthier future market.
Deals that look hot next week include Cell Therapeutics Inc, which develops drugs that use small molecules, and Colonial Downs, according to Fitzgibbon.
